title: Preparing Formula Safely
hook: Powdered formula isn't sterile, so safe prep is about hygiene and getting the ratio exactly right — clean hands and equipment, the correct water-to-powder mix, and fresh feeds made one at a time.
key_points: Wash your hands and use sterilised bottles and equipment for every feed — powdered formula is not sterile.
Follow the exact water-to-powder ratio on the tin: never dilute it or add extra powder.
Make feeds with hot water (per the instructions) to kill bacteria, then cool to body temperature and test on your wrist.
Make feeds fresh one at a time and throw away any formula left after a feed; never reheat in a microwave.
content_html: Infant formula feeds a baby well, but because powdered formula is not sterile, safe preparation is what protects your baby. The NHS stresses two things: hygiene and the right ratio. Wash your hands and use bottles and teats that have been washed and sterilised before each feed, since even sealed tins can contain bacteria that multiply quickly at room temperature.
extra_html: Follow the water-to-powder ratio on the tin exactly — do not dilute it (too little nutrition) or add extra powder (which can cause constipation or dehydration). The NHS method uses freshly boiled water cooled for no more than about 30 minutes so it's still hot enough to kill bacteria, mixed with the powder, then cooled under cold running water and tested on the inside of your wrist until it feels warm, not hot. Make feeds fresh, one at a time, throw away anything left after a feed, and never warm formula in a microwave. This is general guidance; check the instructions on your formula and ask your health visitor if you're unsure.

related.title: Breastfeeding and Formula Both Feed a Baby Well
related.hook: Health bodies recommend breastfeeding where possible, but properly prepared infant formula is a safe, nourishing alternative — a fed baby is the goal.

related.title: Feeding on Demand: Cues and How Often
related.hook: Newborns feed best on demand — watch for early hunger cues rather than the clock, and let wet and dirty diapers, not the exact count of feeds, reassure you they're getting enough.

related.title: Pumping and Storing Breast Milk
related.hook: Expressing milk lets someone else share feeds and keeps supply going when you're back at work. The trick is a simple storage rule — and gentle handling so the milk stays good for baby.

flashcards.prompt: Why does formula need careful, hygienic preparation?

choices.text: Powdered formula is not sterile and can contain bacteria
It improves the flavour for the baby
It makes the powder dissolve faster

flashcards.explanation_html: The NHS notes that even sealed powdered formula can contain bacteria, and bacteria multiply fast at room temperature — so clean hands, sterilised equipment, and hot water for mixing matter.

flashcards.prompt: What should you do with the water-to-powder ratio on the tin?

choices.text: Follow it exactly — never dilute or add extra powder
Add extra powder so baby feels fuller
Add extra water to stretch the tin further

flashcards.explanation_html: Adding extra powder can cause dehydration or constipation; too much water means too few nutrients. Follow the manufacturer's exact ratio.

flashcards.prompt: What do you do with formula left in the bottle after a feed?
flashcards.back_html: Throw it away. Make feeds fresh, one at a time, and never reheat formula in a microwave (it heats unevenly and can scald baby's mouth).
